walkthroughs.title: Arrays are values: copies, reserved capacity and filtering

steps.title: The program entry point
steps.explanation: @main marks LessonMain as the place the program starts, and Swift calls its static main function. The worker compiles with -parse-as-library, which is why an explicit @main type is used instead of top-level statements. main is declared async throws so the same shape works for lessons that await or throw. Each do block below is just a scope that keeps its names separate.
steps.observe: Nothing is printed until the last line of main.

steps.excerpt:
do {
      let original = [1, 2]
      var changed = original
      changed.append(3)
      precondition(original == [1, 2])
      precondition(changed == [1, 2, 3])
    }
steps.title: Changing a copy leaves the original alone
steps.explanation: Swift arrays are value types. var changed = original gives changed its own logical copy, so appending 3 cannot affect original. Behind the scenes Swift uses copy-on-write: both names share one buffer until one of them is mutated, and only then is the buffer copied. precondition stops the program with an error if its condition is false, and it stays active in normal builds.
steps.observe: original is still [1, 2] and changed is [1, 2, 3].

steps.excerpt:
do {
      var values: [Int] = []
      values.reserveCapacity(20)
      precondition(values.count == 0)
      values.append(7)
      precondition(values.count == 1 && values[0] == 7)
    }
steps.title: Capacity is not count
steps.explanation: reserveCapacity(20) asks the array to allocate room for at least 20 elements up front, which avoids repeated reallocation when you know roughly how many items are coming. It does not add any elements, so count is still 0. Only append changes count. Reading values[0] is safe here only because the previous check proved there is exactly one element.
steps.observe: count goes from 0 to 1 and values[0] is 7.

steps.title: filter returns a new array
steps.explanation: filter takes a closure and returns a new array with the elements for which it returns true. $0 is shorthand for the closure's first argument. Because filter builds a new value, source is unchanged, which the second precondition confirms. The task 4 and task 5 blocks follow, and when every precondition holds, print writes the result line.
steps.observe: positives is [2, 4], source keeps its negatives, and the program prints: swift-009: passed

walkthroughs.title: Actors serialize access to their own state

steps.title: A counter actor
steps.explanation: An actor is a reference type that protects its stored properties: only one task at a time can run code inside it. private(set) lets other code read value but only the actor itself can change it. increment needs no lock, because the actor already guarantees that two increments never overlap.
steps.observe: Code outside the actor must use await to call increment or read value.

steps.title: A check-and-update kept inside one actor method
steps.explanation: reserve both checks whether enough stock exists and subtracts it. Because the whole method runs inside the actor without suspending, no other caller can change stock between the guard and the subtraction. guard ... else { return false } is Swift's early exit: the rejection path leaves immediately, and the happy path continues at the outer level.
steps.observe: A request for more than the remaining stock, or a negative amount, returns false and leaves stock unchanged.

steps.title: Twenty concurrent increments
steps.explanation: withTaskGroup starts child tasks and waits for all of them before it returns. Each child awaits counter.increment(). Even though the tasks can run in parallel, the actor runs the increments one at a time, so no update is lost. Reading counter.value from outside also needs await, because it has to wait its turn inside the actor.

steps.title: The second reservation is refused
steps.explanation: Stock starts at 3. The first request for 2 succeeds and leaves 1. The second request for 2 fails the guard. Checking first, second and remaining together shows the full story: one success, one honest refusal, and the correct leftover amount.
steps.observe: first is true, second is false and remaining is 1.

steps.title: A bounded queue actor
steps.explanation: BoundedQueue is declared inside the do block, which Swift allows for local types. offer refuses new items once capacity is reached instead of growing without limit, which is how backpressure is expressed. take returns an optional Int: nil when empty, otherwise the oldest item via removeFirst. The array literal awaits three offers in order.
steps.observe: admitted is [true, true, false], take returns 1, and the program prints: swift-031: passed

steps.title: A Sendable struct
steps.explanation: Sendable marks a type as safe to pass between concurrent tasks. A struct whose stored properties are all immutable lets of Sendable types, here String and Int, qualifies automatically, and the compiler checks the claim. The worker compiles in Swift 6 language mode, where passing a non-Sendable value across tasks is a compile error rather than a warning.
steps.observe: Snapshot has only let properties, so there is no shared mutable state to protect.

steps.title: Capturing a value in a Task
steps.explanation: Task { ... } starts a new unit of concurrent work, and its closure captures snapshot. That capture is allowed because Snapshot is Sendable. await task.value suspends main until the task finishes and then hands back the closure's result.
steps.observe: result is 6, twice the quantity of 3.

steps.title: Results from a task group arrive in any order
steps.explanation: Each child task returns a Snapshot. for await value in group receives results in the order the children finish, which is not guaranteed to match the order they were added. Sorting by name before returning makes the result deterministic, which is the right habit whenever concurrent output feeds a check or a report. map(\.name) uses a key path to pull out each name.
steps.observe: After sorting, the names are a then b on every run.

steps.title: Returning a Sendable summary from a task
steps.explanation: Summary is a local Sendable struct. The task closure declares its return type explicitly with () -> Summary, builds an array, and returns its count and total. reduce(0, +) starts at 0 and adds each element. Because Summary is Sendable, the value can safely come back to main.
steps.observe: count is 3 and total is 9, and the program prints: swift-033: passed
